book_context: A 1915 prologue of the Lusitania hand-off is followed by the post-war comic thriller. Tommy and Tuppence form a 'joint venture'. A chance-overheard name, Jane Finn, triggers Whittington's panic, and that leads to Carter, Julius and Mr. Brown. Recurring mechanisms include: advertisements; coincidence as a theme; bluffing about how much one knows; money and marriage talk that pays off in two proposals; the hidden master criminal who uses 'Brown' and plays nonentities. Planted details pay off later: the clerk Brown, Rita, the Paris pensionnat, the Esthonia firm, the green toque, the hospital meeting and Tommy's uncle. In early chapters the girl's identity, Danvers's name and Brown's identity must not be disclosed beyond what the text shows.
continuity_checks: The Whittington identification rests only on Tommy's vague description of the first man; the second man remains undescribed.
No speculation about the clerk Brown or the meaning of 'Jane Finn'.
The pencil is borrowed back from Tommy, consistent with the earlier chapters.

essential: Taxi fare scramble: Tommy's limited coins and the driver's protest. Tuppence claims nothing smaller than a fiver, and the truth isn't believed.
She proposes extravagant lunch spots and an absurd menu. Tommy is incredulous, and she waves five-pound notes. They lunch at the Piccadilly grill room.

She tells the story and says she invented 'Jane Finn'. Tommy corrects her: he told her the name. One of the two men he overheard was big, fat, clean-shaven and dark, so Tuppence identifies Whittington. Tommy did not notice the other man.
Tommy turns serious: she can't bluff forever, and it may be actionable blackmail. She rebuts with her definition of blackmail.

Tuppence's plan: she goes alone tomorrow to stall Whittington, while Tommy, whom Whittington barely saw, waits outside and follows him on her signal. Tommy objects to 'one young man is much like another' ('the second time').
Tommy limits her spending plans. They have dinner and a show, and two fivers are spent.
Next morning the office is shut. A clerk says the company closed yesterday afternoon and is being wound up, the office is to let, and no address is known.
Tuppence argues their flight proves the Jane Finn business matters: 'sleuths in earnest'. Tommy notes there's no one left to sleuth.
She borrows the pencil and writes the new ad, signed Y. A.
optional: Fishers banter and 'Even so, O King' (p17–21).
Bus in Piccadilly Circus and choosing the grill room (p23–28).

verbatim.text: “No. _I_ told it to you. Don’t you remember, I said yesterday I’d overheard two people talking about a female called Jane Finn?
“And people say that coincidences don’t happen!”
Blackmail is saying you’ll tell unless you are given money. Now, there’s nothing I could tell, because I don’t really know anything.
After all, one young man is much like another.
“Can’t it, though!” Tuppence’s little chin shot out defiantly. “Do you think this is the end? If so, you’re wrong. It’s just the beginning!”

voice_profile: Brisk, light omniscient narration that mostly yields to dialogue. Comedy comes from post-war slang ('old bean', 'stony', 'rag'), mock-formal narratorial labels ('Mr. Beresford magnificently', 'Miss Cowley told him'), and running jokes with setup and payoff. Tuppence is impulsive, mercenary in speech and quick at bluffing. Tommy is slow, dry and deflating. Exposition is kept spare. Suspense is planted through small, casual details: a name overheard, a clerk's name, a telephone message. Chapters often end on a cliffhanger line of dialogue. The prologue uses a graver register: plain, urgent, with short exchanges.
